c.tagline: Scottish-founded city of Victorian grandeur, students and wild Otago coast.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are metered; Dunedin Taxis and Southern Taxis are the main operators, and Uber also operates in the city.

emergency.note: 111 is the single emergency number for police, fire and ambulance across New Zealand; Dunedin Hospital runs the main public emergency department.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Rowdy student parties around North Dunedin's Castle Street on big weekends; otherwise usual awareness.

hood_desc: The civic heart around the eight-sided Octagon plaza, ringed by the Dunedin Railway Station, cafes, bars and galleries; the most central, walkable base for first-time visitors.
The lively student quarter around the University of Otago's bluestone campus and North East Valley, full of cheap eats, flats and pubs; suits younger travellers and a budget stay near the action.
Dunedin's seaside suburbs on a long surf beach, with the St Clair saltwater pool, esplanade cafes and coastal walks; a relaxed, scenic base for those wanting the coast over the city.
A revived heritage precinct of Victorian warehouses on Vogel and lower Stuart Streets, now home to design studios, craft coffee, street art and small bars; best for a creative, indie vibe.
A historic deep-water port village about 15 km from the centre, with steep streets, galleries, seafood and cruise-ship bustle; a quiet, artsy escape with harbour views.
lodging: Majestic Mansions Apartments at St Clair

water.note: Tap water is safe and excellent quality.

transit.hours: Orbus buses run roughly 7am to around 11pm on weekdays with reduced weekend and evening services; there is no rail or night network, so taxis and Uber cover late hours.
transit.note: Dunedin's public transport is the Orbus bus network run by the Otago Regional Council; there are no trains or trams, and the compact city centre is easily walked.
transit.pay: Tap on and off with a prepaid Bee Card (sold at the bus hub and retailers) for the cheapest fares, or pay the driver with cash; contactless bank-card payment is also accepted on board.

bus: InterCity coach services to Christchurch, Queenstown and Invercargill
Atomic Travel and other regional coaches
train: Dunedin Railways scenic excursions (Taieri Gorge / Seasider) — tourist services only, no scheduled passenger rail

transit.m: Super Shuttle door-to-door shared van to the city centre (~30-40 min)
Private airport transfer / coach connection to central Dunedin

tip.r: Tipping is not customary in New Zealand; rounding up or leaving ~10% for exceptional service is appreciated but never expected.

food.name: Cheese rolls
food.desc: Southern sushi - white bread spread with a cheese, onion soup mix and evaporated milk filling, rolled up, toasted and dripping with butter.

places.name: Otago Farmers Market
places.note: Saturday morning market stalls turn out hot cheese rolls by the tray; the local benchmark version.

places.name: No.7 Balmac
places.note: Long-standing neighbourhood bistro whose cheese rolls are regularly named among the best in the country.

places.name: The Perc Cafe
places.note: Veteran city cafe serving cheese rolls with soup all through the Otago winter.

food.name: Blue cod and chips
food.desc: Sweet, firm southern blue cod in a light batter with hot chips - the fish Otago and Southland argue about and everyone orders anyway.

places.name: Best Cafe
places.note: Dunedin fish and chip institution since the 1930s; blue cod, chowder and oysters in season.

places.name: The Fish Hook
places.note: Fish shop and eat-in counter for blue cod, tarakihi and groper cooked to order.

places.name: Speight's Ale House
places.note: Southern pub classics beside the brewery; battered blue cod with a Speight's on the side.

food.name: Bluff oysters
food.desc: Fat, briny wild oysters dredged from Foveaux Strait, served raw on ice or lightly crumbed - a short, fiercely anticipated season from March to August.

places.name: Best Cafe
places.note: Sells Bluff oysters raw and crumbed the moment the season opens; queues follow.

places.name: Otago Farmers Market
places.note: Seafood stalls carry Bluff oysters and other southern kaimoana during the season.

places.name: Speight's Ale House
places.note: Puts Bluff oysters on the specials board in season alongside the standard southern menu.

food.name: Seafood chowder
food.desc: Thick creamy chowder loaded with blue cod, mussels and smoked fish, served with buttered bread - the standard southern lunch on a cold Dunedin day.

places.name: Best Cafe
places.note: Its chowder is close to legendary locally and comes packed with fish rather than potato.

places.name: Speight's Ale House
places.note: Hearty pub version in a warm wood-panelled room, ideal in winter.

places.name: Ombrellos Kitchen and Bar
places.note: Cosy student-quarter gastropub known for comfort cooking and generous chowder.

food.name: Central Otago lamb and venison
food.desc: Grass-fed lamb rack and farmed Otago venison, roasted rare and plated with root vegetables - the inland half of the region's larder.

places.name: Speight's Ale House
places.note: Lamb shanks, steak and venison done plainly and well; the reliable southern-fare choice.

places.name: Bracken Restaurant
places.note: Dunedin's fine-dining stalwart, degustation menus built on Otago meat and produce.

places.name: No.7 Balmac
places.note: Neighbourhood bistro with a regional menu that leans on Otago lamb and game.

food.name: Whitebait fritters
food.desc: Tiny translucent whitebait bound with egg and fried into a fritter, served with lemon and white bread - a short and expensive spring delicacy.

places.name: Best Cafe
places.note: Seasonal whitebait appears here first; ask, as supply is weather dependent.

places.name: Otago Farmers Market
places.note: Fish stalls sell fresh whitebait during the spring run for cooking yourself.

places.name: Ombrellos Kitchen and Bar
places.note: Runs whitebait and other seasonal southern specials when the run is on.

food.name: Speight's and Emerson's beer
food.desc: Speight's Gold Medal Ale has been brewed in Dunedin since 1876; Emerson's pioneered New Zealand craft beer in the same city a century later.

places.name: Speight's Ale House
places.note: Attached to the historic brewery, with limited Speight's brews poured nowhere else in the country.

places.name: Emerson's Brewery
places.note: Purpose-built taproom and restaurant pouring the full Emerson's range fresh from the tanks.

places.name: Vault 21
places.note: Central bar and kitchen with a wide New Zealand craft tap list in the middle of town.

food.name: Central Otago pinot noir
food.desc: Bannockburn, Gibbston and Bendigo pinot noir from the world's southernmost wine region - dark cherry and thyme, an hour or two inland from the city.

places.name: Vault 21
places.note: Central wine list strong on Central Otago producers, with plenty available by the glass.

places.name: Bracken Restaurant
places.note: Regional wine matches built around Central Otago pinot for each degustation course.

places.name: No.7 Balmac
places.note: Well-kept Otago-focused cellar in a relaxed suburban dining room.

landmarks: Dunedin Railway Station
A Flemish Renaissance extravagance of black basalt and white Oamaru stone, mosaic floors and stained glass, reputedly New Zealand's most photographed building.
Larnach Castle
New Zealand's only castle crowns the Otago Peninsula with Gothic Revival grandeur, scandal-laden history and glorious gardens overlooking the harbour.
Taiaroa Head and the Royal Albatross Centre
At the peninsula's wild tip lives the world's only mainland breeding colony of northern royal albatross, wingspans three metres wide.
Baldwin Street
Officially the world's steepest residential street, a 35-percent gradient that lures visitors to puff up its short, absurd incline for photos.
The Octagon and St Paul's Cathedral
Dunedin's eight-sided civic heart gathers the Gothic cathedral, ornate municipal chambers, a Robbie Burns statue and buzzing café terraces.
Tunnel Beach
A dramatic clifftop walk descends through a hand-hewn Victorian tunnel to a hidden cove of sandstone arches and thundering surf.
Tūhura Otago Museum
The city's grand museum spans Māori taonga, Pacific voyaging and natural history, plus a live tropical butterfly rainforest.
Toitū Otago Settlers Museum
An engaging social-history museum telling Dunedin's story from Kāi Tahu origins through Scottish settlement and gold-rush boom years.
Dunedin Botanic Garden
New Zealand's oldest botanic garden climbs Signal Hill's lower slopes with world-class rhododendrons, an aviary and century-old trees.
St Clair Beach and Esplanade
Dunedin's surf beach pairs rolling southern-ocean breakers with a heated saltwater pool and a strip of relaxed esplanade cafés.

train.note: New Zealand is an island nation with no international trains, and Dunedin has no scheduled passenger rail. The historic Dunedin Railway Station is instead the base for Dunedin Railways scenic tourist excursions (https://www.dunedinrailways.co.nz/) such as the Taieri Gorge and coastal Seasider trips.

bus.note: No international coaches. InterCity (https://www.intercity.co.nz/) is the main long-distance bus network, linking Dunedin north to Christchurch, inland to Queenstown and south to Invercargill; smaller operators such as Atomic Travel run similar routes.

ferry.note: No scheduled passenger ferries. Dunedin's Port Otago at Port Chalmers is a cargo and cruise port; the only regular boat trips are wildlife and harbour cruises on Otago Harbour.

half.name: Moeraki Boulders
half.blurb: Large spherical concretions weathered out of Paleocene mudstone on Koekohe Beach, tied in Māori legend to a canoe wreck.
